practiceSet.title: U2.LT1 Practice: Atoms, Molecules, and Bonds
practiceSet.description: Practice protons, neutrons, and electrons, ions and isotopes, the six main elements of life, telling elements, molecules, and compounds apart, reading chemical formulas, and ionic, covalent, and hydrogen bonds.

activity.title: U2.LT1 Relearning: Atoms, Molecules, and Bonds
activity.content:
**What you need to be able to do:** I can describe atoms, elements, molecules, compounds, and types of chemical bonds.

**Think of LEGO bricks.** One brick is an atom: the smallest piece that still counts as that kind of brick. A bin of only red bricks is an element. Snap two or more bricks together and you have a molecule. If the bricks you snapped together are different colors, it is also a compound. The way the bricks click together is the bond.

**The atom.** An atom is the smallest unit of matter that keeps an element's properties. Its center, the **nucleus**, holds **protons (+)** and **neutrons (0)**. **Electrons (−)** move in energy levels (shells) around the nucleus. The first shell holds up to 2 electrons, and the second holds up to 8, so fill the first shell before you start the second. The number of protons is the **atomic number**, and it decides which element the atom is (carbon always has 6). Neutrons add mass. Electrons form bonds. A neutral atom has the same number of protons and electrons.

**Ions and isotopes.** An **ion** has a different number of electrons, so it has a charge: lose electrons → positive (Na⁺), gain electrons → negative (Cl⁻). An **isotope** has a different number of neutrons: carbon-12 has 6 neutrons and carbon-14 has 8. The number in an isotope's name (its mass number) is protons + neutrons: carbon-14 has 6 + 8 = 14. Same protons, same chemistry, different mass. Changing the number of protons makes a different element.

**Elements and CHNOPS.** An **element** is a pure substance made of only one kind of atom. Six elements make up about 99% of living things: **C**arbon (backbone of every macromolecule), **H**ydrogen (most common atom in the body), **N**itrogen (proteins and DNA), **O**xygen (water and respiration), **P**hosphorus (DNA, ATP, cell membranes), and **S**ulfur (some proteins).

**Molecules and compounds.** A **molecule** is two or more atoms held together by chemical bonds, and the atoms can be the same element (O₂). A **compound** is two or more **different** elements bonded in a fixed ratio (H₂O, NaCl, CO₂, C₆H₁₂O₆, but not O₂). A compound's properties are different from its elements' properties. A chemical formula shows the kinds and numbers of atoms: C₆H₁₂O₆ = 6 carbon, 12 hydrogen, 6 oxygen. A **structural formula** goes one step further and shows which atoms are bonded to which, with a line for each bond: water is H–O–H.

**Three kinds of bonds.**
- **Ionic bond:** electrons are **transferred** from one atom to another, and the opposite charges attract (Na⁺Cl⁻ in table salt; calcium phosphate, the hard mineral in bones and teeth).
- **Covalent bond:** electrons are **shared**. Strong. Builds every molecule in the body (H–O–H in water, C–C chains in sugars and fats).
- **Hydrogen bond:** a **weak** attraction between molecules: a slightly positive H pulled toward a slightly negative O or N (water sticking to water, the two strands of DNA).

**Worked example 1:** An atom has 6 protons, 7 neutrons, and 6 electrons. What is it? Step 1: Protons decide the element: 6 protons = carbon. Step 2: Protons (6) = electrons (6), so the charges cancel; it is not an ion. Step 3: Carbon-12 has 6 neutrons, and this atom has 7, so it is an isotope: 6 + 7 = 13, carbon-13. **Answer:** a neutral carbon-13 atom, an isotope of carbon.

**Worked example 2:** Is methane, CH₄, an element, a molecule, a compound, or more than one? Step 1: Its atoms are bonded together, so it is a molecule. Step 2: It has two different elements (C and H), so it is also a compound. Step 3: It has more than one kind of atom, so it is not an element. **Answer:** both a molecule and a compound (5 atoms: 1 carbon + 4 hydrogen).

**Worked example 3:** You sprinkle salt crystals into a glass of water. Before they dissolve, what bonds are at work? Step 1: A salt crystal is Na⁺ and Cl⁻. Sodium gave an electron to chlorine, and the opposite charges attract: ionic. Step 2: Inside each water molecule, O and H share electrons: covalent. Step 3: Separate water molecules attract each other: hydrogen bonds. **Answer:** ionic bonds in the salt crystals, covalent bonds inside each water molecule, and hydrogen bonds between water molecules. Once the salt dissolves, water molecules pull the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ apart, so those ionic bonds break.

**Watch out for:** mixing up ions (electrons change) and isotopes (neutrons change); thinking a change in protons makes an ion (it makes a different element); calling O₂ a compound (it has only one element); reading P as potassium (P is phosphorus, potassium is K); saying ionic bonds share electrons (they transfer them); and calling hydrogen bonds strong (they are weak, but there are a lot of them).
prompts: Draw a Bohr model of a neutral atom with 8 protons and 8 neutrons (fill the first shell before the second). Label the nucleus, the protons, the neutrons, the electrons, and the charge of each particle. Name the element.
Explain the difference between an ion and an isotope. Give one example of each from the notes.
Sort these into three groups (element, molecule of one element, compound): C, O₂, H₂O, N₂, NaCl, C₆H₁₂O₆. Explain the rule you used for each group.
Compare ionic, covalent, and hydrogen bonds. For each one, tell what happens with the electrons and give one example from living things.
